newsitem.title: USA: Dollar nears 6-year peak vs mark as euro doubts flare.
newsitem.headline: Dollar nears 6-year peak vs mark as euro doubts flare.

text.p: The dollar approached its highest level against the German mark in roughly six years on Wednesday amid doubts about the strength of Europe's planned single currency and lingering weakness in the German economy.
Poor economic performance in Germany and other Continental European countries has contrasted starkly with the comparative economic nirvana of steady growth and low inflation in the United States.

This backdrop has made for a rocky road in Europe's drive to launch the euro by the beginning of 1999 and sparked mounting scepticism about the strength of the currency, which is scheduled to replace the normally reliable and rock-solid mark.

It has also translated into a steady rise in the dollar against the mark, which has suffered as prospects for a broad, inclusive monetary union -- including countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal -- have grown.
On Wednesday, the dollar pushed to a peak of 1.7655 marks, its highest level against the German currency in roughly 3-1/2 years.

A move above 1.7686 marks, which is now within striking distance, would take the dollar to its top level since August 1991 and open the door for a push to 1.80 marks and perhaps 2.0 marks per dollar, market pros said.
The last time the dollar fetched 2 marks was in September 1989, just before the dismantling of the Berlin Wall.
"Some people say that all the good news is already priced into the dollar," said Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in New York.

"But the foreign exchange market has a crowd-like mentality and right now the momentum is feeding on itself," he added. "It takes something dramatic to break that and I don't see anything on the horizon to do so."
In addition to a strong economy, a number of other factors are working in the dollar's favour.

The U.S. stock market is setting new records on almost a daily basis and long-term government bond yields, which act as a benchmark for mortgage rates and consumer loans, have slid to almost 6.5 percent from over 7.0 percent in late May.

Highlighting the contrast with Germany, Chandler noted, was the fact that the top 100 German companies saw their profit margins shrink by 5 percent last year while the top U.S. companies saw their profit margins grow by 30 percent.
German officials have also expressed little dissatisfaction with the mark's weakness against the dollar, a development which has helped the country's competitiveness on global markets.

"I believe in some respects that Europe condones a higher dollar as a way to stimulate their own export markets," said John McCarthy, a senior vice president on the foreign exchange trading desk at ING Barings Capital Markets.

Exports have been a rare source of strength for the economies of Germany and its European neighbours. On Tuesday, Germany reported that its unemployment total grew by 11,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.37 million in June, levels not seen since World War II.
Germany's persistent unemployment problem has frustrated efforts to curb public spending in order to meet the strict economic criteria for entry into monetary union.

And recent elections in France, which gave new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin a mandate to fight massive unemployment there, have sapped confidence in the ability of the single currency's leading proponents to meet the guidelines.
As a result, prospects for a weakening of the criteria and a broader group of founding members for the euro have grown, pushing the mark lower.
"It's no longer so much a question of whether EMU will take place but whether the whole process is becoming a bit too sloppy," said McCarthy.
"That would suggest that down the road it will be a sloppy, weak, undisciplined currency and the market is negative on the deutsche mark in reflection of that."
